question.html:
A 450-lb load hangs from the corner $C$ of a rigid piece of pipe $ABCD$ that has been bent as shown. The pipe is supported by ball-and-socket joints $A$ and $D$, and by a cable attached at the midpoint $E$ of the portion $BC$ of the pipe and at point $G$ on the wall. Determine (a) where $G$ should be located if the tension in the cable is to be minimum, (b) the corresponding minimum value of tension.

The x-coordinate of the location of G ($G_X$) is equal to:

The y-coordinate of the location of G ($G_Y$) is equal to:

The minimum value of tension ($T_{min}$) is equal to:
solution.html:
Draw the free-body diagram of the pipe showing the reactions at $A$ and $D$. Isolate the unknown tension $T$ and the known weight $W$ by summing moments about the diagonal line $AD$, and compute values from the equilibrium equations. The vector expression of line AB $\overline{AB}$ $\implies$ $\hat{r_{BC}} = [(12\hat{i} + 12\hat{j} - 6\hat{k})]/[\sqrt(18)]$ = ($\frac{2}{3}\hat{i} + \frac{2}{3}\hat{j} + -\frac{1}{3}\hat{k}$)
  • $\implies \overrightarrow{AC} \times W = (12\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}) \times (-450j) = -5400k$
  • $\hat{r_{BC}} \cdot (\overrightarrow{AC} \times W) = (\frac{2}{3}\hat{i} + \frac{2}{3}\hat{j} + -\frac{1}{3}\hat{k}) \cdot (-5400k) = +1800 $ $\textbf{(2)}$

Recalling the commutative property for mixed triple products, you can rewrite the last equation in the form

  • $T \cdot (\hat{r_{BC}} \times \overrightarrow{AE}) = -1800 lb \cdot ft$ $\textbf{(3)}$
  • This shows that the projection of $T$ on the vector $\hat{r_{BC}} \times \overrightarrow{AE}$ is a constant. It follows that $T$ is minimum when it is parallel to the vector
  • $\implies \hat{r_{BC}} \times \overrightarrow{AE} = (\frac{2}{3}\hat{i} + \frac{2}{3}\hat{j} + -\frac{1}{3}\hat{k}) \times (6i + 12j) = 4i - 2j + 4k$
  • The corresponding unit vector is $(\frac{2}{3}i - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{3}k)$ which yields
  • $\implies T_{min} = T(\frac{2}{3}i - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{3}k)$ $\textbf{(4)}$
  • Substituting for $T$ and $\hat{r_{BC}}$ in Eq. (3) and computing dot products yields $T = -300$, carrying this value into Eq.(4)
  • $\implies T_{min} = 300 lb$
  • Since the vector $\overrightarrow{EG}$ and the force $T_{min}$ have the same direction, their components must be proportional.
  • Denoting the coordinates of G by x,y, and 0, you get
  • $\frac{x-6}{-200} = \frac{y-12}{+100} = \frac{0-6}{-200}$
  • $\implies x = 0, y = 15 ft

question.html:
A uniform pipe cover of radius $ r = 240 mm$ and mass $30 kg$ is held in a horizontal position by the cable $CD$. Assuming that the bearing at $B$ does not exert any axial thrust, determine the tension in the cable and the reactions at $A$ and $B$.

The magnitude of the tension in cable $CD$ ($T_{CD}$) is:

The x-component of the reaction at point A ($A_X$) is equal to:

The y-component of the reaction at point A ($A_Y$) is equal to:

The z-component of the reaction at point A ($A_Z$) is equal to:

The x-component of the reaction at point B ($B_X$) is equal to:

The y-component of the reaction at point B ($B_Y$) is equal to:

The z-component of the reaction at point B ($B_Z$) is equal to:
solution.html:
Draw a free-body diagram with the coordinate axes shown and express the unknown cable tension as a Cartesian vector. Then apply the equilibrium equations ($\Sigma F_{xyz} = 0$ and $\Sigma M_{xyz} = 0$ ) to determine this tension and the support reactions. The forces acting on the free body include its weight, which is
  • $W = -mg\hat{j} = (-294 N) \hat{j}$

Express the components of $\mathbf{T}$ in terms of the unknown magnitude T by resolving the vector $\overrightarrow{DC}$ into rectangular components:

  • $\overrightarrow{DC} = -(480 mm)\hat{i} + (240 mm)\hat{j} - (160 mm)\hat{k} \implies$ $DC$ = 560 mm
  • $\mathbf{T}$ = $T$$\frac{\overrightarrow{DC}}{DC}$ = $-\frac{6}{7}T\hat{i} + \frac{3}{7}T\hat{j} - \frac{2}{7}T\hat{k}$
  • Applying equilibirum conditions ($\Sigma F = 0$)
  • $ A_{x}\hat{i} + A_{y}\hat{j} + A_{z}\hat{k} + B_{x}\hat{i} + B_{y}\hat{j} + \mathbf{T} - (294 N)\hat{j}$
  • $(A_{x} + B_{x} - \frac{6}{7}T)\hat{i} + (A_{y} + B_{y} + \frac{3}{7}T - 294 N) \hat{j} + (A_{z} -\frac{2}{7}T)\hat{k} = 0$ $\textbf{(Eq. 1)}$

What equilibrium equation should you use next considering what forces are creating moments about points $A$ and $B$. Which equation will be easier to solve?
  • $\Sigma M_{B} = \Sigma(r \times F) = 0$:
  • $\implies 2r\hat{k} \times (A_{x}\hat{i} + A_{y}\hat{j} + A_{z}\hat{k}) + (2r\hat{i} + r\hat{k}) \times (-\frac{6}{7}T\hat{i} + \frac{3}{7}T\hat{j} - \frac{2}{7}T\hat{k}) + (r\hat{i} + r\hat{k}) \times (-294 N)\hat{j}$
  • $\implies (-2A_{y} - \frac{3}{7}T + 294 N)r\hat{i} + (2A_{x} - \frac{2}{7})r\hat{j} + (\frac{6}{7}T - 294 N)r\hat{k} $ $\textbf{(Eq. 2)}$
  • Setting the coefficients of the unit vectors equal to zero in Eq. 2 gives three scalar equations, which yield
  • $A_{x} = +49 N$
  • $A_{y} = +73.5 N$
  • $\implies T = 343 N$
  • Setting the coefficients of the unit vectors equal to zero in Eq. 1 produces three more scalar equations. After substituting the values of $T, A_{x},$ and $A_{y}$ into these equations you obtain:
  • $A_{z} = +98.0 N$
  • $B_{x} = +245 N$
  • $B_{y} = +73.5 N$
  • The reactions at $A$ and $B$ are therefore
  • $A = +(49 N)\hat{i} + (73.5)\hat{j} + (98 N)\hat{k}$
  • $B = +(245 N)\hat{i} + (73.5)\hat{j} + (0 N)\hat{k}$

question.html:
Determine the components of reaction at the ball-and-socket joint A and the tension in each cable necessary for equilibrium of the rod.

The x-component of the reaction force at A ($A_x$) is equal to:

The y-component of the reaction force at A ($A_y$) is equal to:

The z-component of the reaction force at A ($A_z$) is equal to:

The force of tension acting along cable BC ($T_{BC}$) is equal to:

The force of tension acting along cable BD ($T_{BD}$) is equal to:
solution.html:
3D equilibrium dictates $\Sigma F_x = 0$, $\Sigma F_y = 0$, $\Sigma F_z = 0$, $\Sigma M_{sum} = 0$. Deconstruct the given forces into their vector expressions, recalling the formula for vector expression involving the vector's magnitude and the unit vector. Hint: $\vec{T}_{BC} = T_{BC}(\frac{\vec{BC}}{BC})$ Using $\Sigma M_B = 0$ allows you to consider only forces acting perpendicular to point B and solve for reaction forces acting at point A.
  • Notice the symmetry of $T_{BC}$ and $T_{BD}$, once you derive the vector equation for one cable, the y-component of the other will have the opposite sign.
  • $\vec{T}_{BC} = T_{BC}(\frac{\vec{BC}}{BC}) = T_{BC}(\frac{-6\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}}{7})$
  • $\vec{T}_{BC} = -0.857T_{BC}\hat{i}-0.286T_{BC}\hat{j}+0.429T_{BC}\hat{k}$
  • $\vec{T}_{BD} = -0.857T_{BC}\hat{i}+0.286T_{BC}\hat{j}+0.429T_{BC}\hat{k}$
  • Now we must consider the other forces acting upon the rod and their vector expressions
  • $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{z}$
  • $\vec{W} = -600\hat{k}$
  • Recall $\Sigma M_B = 0$, which allows us to solve for forces creating a moment about B
  • $(-6\hat{i} \times A_{z}\hat{k}) + (-6\hat{i} \times A_{y}\hat{j}) + (-3\hat{i} \times -600\hat{k})$
  • $(6A_{z} - 1800)\hat{j} - 6A_{y}\hat{k} = 0$
  • Solving for $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{z}$ direction $\implies$ $A_{z} = 300 N$ and $A_{y} = 0 N$
  • Recall $\Sigma F_y = 0$, and summing the y-components of $\vec{T}_{BC}$, $\vec{T}_{BD}$, and reaction forces yields
  • $-0.286T_{BC} + 0.286T_{BD} + A_y = 0$
  • $T_{BC} = T_{BD}$
  • Repeating the process for the x-direction ($\Sigma F_x = 0$) yields:
  • $-0.857T_{BC} - 0.857T_{BD} + A_x = 0$
  • $-2(0.857)T_{BC} = -A_x$
  • Finally for the summation of forces in the z-direction ($\Sigma F_z = 0$):
  • $0.429 T_{BC} + 0.429T_{BD} + A_z - 600 = 0$
  • $2(0.429)T_{BC} = 300$
  • $\implies T_{BC} = T_{BD} = 350 N$
  • $A_x = 2(0.857)(350) \implies 600 N$

Due to an unequal distribution of fuel in the wing tanks, the centers of gravity for airplane fuselage $A$ and wings $B$ and $C$ are located as shown. If these components have weights $W_A$ = 45,000 lb, $W_B$ = 8,000 lb, $W_C$ = 6,000 lb, determine the normal reactions of the wheels $D$, $E$, and $F$ on the ground. Round your answer to the nearest whole number.

The magnitude of the reaction force at point D ($R_D$) is equal to:

The magnitude of the reaction force at point F ($R_F$) is equal to:

The magnitude of the reaction force at point D ($R_E$) is equal to:
solution.html:
3D equilibrium dictates $\Sigma F_x = 0$, $\Sigma F_y = 0$, $\Sigma F_z = 0$, $\Sigma M_{sum} = 0$. Deconstruct the given forces into their vector expressions, and consider the moments created by the given forces. Using $\Sigma M_x = 0$ allows you to consider only forces creating a moment about the x-axis, and solve for the normal reactions.

$*Note*$ The symmetry of wheels $E$ and $D$ indicates that their induced moments will be opposite signs (counter-clockwise & clockwise).
  • $\Sigma M_{F} = 0 \implies -(14 \times R_{D}) + (14 \times R_{E}) + (8000 \times 6) - (6000 \times 8) = 0$
  • $-14R_{D} + 14R_{E} = 0$
  • $\implies R_{D} = R_{E}$
  • $\Sigma M_{y} = 0 \implies -(27 \times R_{F}) + (4500 \times 7) +(8000 \times 4) + (6000 \times 4) = 0$
  • $-27R_{F} + 371000 = 0$
  • $R_{F} = \frac{-371000}{-27}$
  • $\implies R_{F} = 13741$ lb

$*Note*$ $\Sigma M_{Z} = 0$ does not allow us to solve for any unknown variables given all forces are parallel to the rotational axis of the z-axis. Instead, utilize the summation of forces in the z-direction ($\Sigma F_{Z} = 0$)

  • $\Sigma F_{Z} = 0$
  • $R_{F} + R_{D} + R{E} - 4500 - 8000 - 6000 = 0$
  • $13741 + 2R_{E} -4500 - 8000 - 6000= 0$
  • $2R_{E} -45260= 0$
  • $R_E = \frac{45260}{2}$
  • $\implies R_{D} = R_{E} = 22630$ lb

question.html:
A 20-kg ladder used to reach high shelves in a storeroom is supported by two flanged wheels $A$ and $B$ mounted on a rail and by a flangeless wheel $C$ resting against a rail fixed to the wall. An 80-kg man stands on the ladder and leans to the right. The line of action of the combined weight $\textbf{W}$ of the man and ladder intersects the floor at point $D$. Determine the reactions at $A,B,$ and $C$

The x-component of the reaction at point A ($A_X$) is equal to:

The y-component of the reaction at point A ($A_Y$) is equal to:

The z-component of the reaction at point A ($A_Z$) is equal to:

The x-component of the reaction at point B ($B_X$) is equal to:

The y-component of the reaction at point B ($B_Y$) is equal to:

The z-component of the reaction at point B ($B_Z$) is equal to:

The x-component of the reaction at point C ($C_X$) is equal to:

The y-component of the reaction at point C ($B_Y$) is equal to:

The z-component of the reaction at point B ($B_Z$) is equal to:
solution.html:
Draw a free-body diagram of the ladder, then write and solve the equilibrium equations in three dimensions. The combined weight of the man and the ladder is:
  • $W = -mg\hat{j} = (-981 N) \hat{j}$

You have five unknown reaction components: two at each flanged wheel and one at teh flangeless wheel. The ladder is thus only partially constrained; it is free to roll along the rails. It is, however, in equiibrium under the given load because the equation $\Sigma F_{x} = 0$ is satisfied.

  • Applying equilibirum conditions ($\Sigma F = 0$)
  • $ A_{y}\hat{j} + A_{z}\hat{k} + B_{y}\hat{j} + B_{z}\hat{k} - (981 N)\hat{j} + C\hat{k} = 0$ $textbf{(Eq. 1)}$

What equilibrium equation should you use next considering what forces are creating moments about points $A$, $B$, and $C$. Which equation will be easier to solve?
  • $\Sigma M_{B} = \Sigma(r \times F) = 0$:
  • $\implies 1.2\hat{i} \times ( B_{y}\hat{j} + B_{z}\hat{k}) + (0.9\hat{i} - 0.6\hat{k}) \times (-981\hat{j}) + (0.6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 1.2\hat{k}) \times (C\hat{k})$
  • Computing the vector products yields:
  • $\implies 1.2B_{y}\hat{k} - 1.2B_{z}\hat{j} - 883\hat{k} - 589\hat{i} - 0.6C\hat{j} + 3C\hat{i} = 0$
  • $\implies (3C - 589)\hat{i} - (1.2B_{z} + 0.6C)\hat{j} + (1.2B_{y} - 883)\hat{k} = 0$ $\textbf{(Eq. 2)}$
  • Setting the coefficients of $i, j, $ and $k$ equal to zero in Eq. 2 produces the following three scalar equations, all of which state the sum of the moments about each coordinate axis must be zero:
  • $3C - 589 = 0 \implies C = +196 N$
  • $1.2B_{z} + 0.6C = 0 \implies B_{z} = -98 N$
  • $1.2B_{y} - 883 = 0 \implies B_{y} = +736 N$
  • The reactions at $B$ and $C$ are therefore
  • $B = (736 N)\hat{j} - (98 N)\hat{k}$
  • $C = (196 N)\hat{k}$
  • Setting the coefficients of $j$ and $k$ equal to zero, and plugging in $B_{y}, B_{z},$ and $C$ in Eq. 1 allows you to solve for the reaction components at A:
  • $\implies A = (+245 N)\hat{j} - (98.1 N)\hat{k}$

A sum of ${{params.principal}} is borrowed at an interest rate of {{params.interestRate}}% per year.

 Calculate the amount owed after 1 year if the interest is compounded monthly. Calculate the amount owed after 1 year if the interest is compounded weekly. Calculate the amount owed after 1 year if the interest is compounded daily.
solution.html:
To calculate the amount owed after 1 year with different compounding frequencies, we will use the formula for compound interest: \[ A = P \left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt} \] where:
  • \(A\) is the amount of money accumulated after n years, including interest.
  • \(P\) is the principal amount (the initial sum of money).
  • \(r\) is the annual interest rate (decimal).
  • \(n\) is the number of times that interest is compounded per year.
  • \(t\) is the time the money is invested or borrowed for, in years.
 For monthly compounding, we have \(n = 12\). The formula becomes: \[ A_{monthly} = P \left(1 + \frac{r}{12}\right)^{12 \times 1} \] Substituting \(P = {{params.principal}}\) and \(r = \frac{ {{params.interestRate}} }{100}\) gives: \[ A_{monthly} = {{params.principal}} \left(1 + \frac{\frac{ {{params.interestRate}} }{100} }{12}\right)^{12} \] For weekly compounding, we have \(n = 52\). The formula becomes: \[ A_{weekly} = P \left(1 + \frac{r}{52}\right)^{52 \times 1} \] Substituting gives: \[ A_{weekly} = {{params.principal}} \left(1 + \frac{\frac{ {{params.interestRate}} }{100} }{52}\right)^{52} \] For daily compounding, we have \(n = 365\). The formula becomes: \[ A_{daily} = P \left(1 + \frac{r}{365}\right)^{365 \times 1} \] Substituting gives: \[ A_{daily} = {{params.principal}} \left(1 + \frac{\frac{ {{params.interestRate}} }{100} }{365}\right)^{365} \] Thus, the amounts owed after 1 year for monthly, weekly, and daily compounding are respectively:
  • Monthly Compounding: \(A_{monthly}\)
  • Weekly Compounding: \(A_{weekly}\)
  • Daily Compounding: \(A_{daily}\)

question.html:
You take out a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage for a house. The amount borrowed is {{params.P}} USD. The interest rate is {{params.i}}% per year compounded monthly. You decide to sell the house immediately after the {{params.t}}th payment

How much do you still owe on the loan?

What is the total amount you have paid the lender by the time you sell the house?

How much principal have you paid the lender by the time you sell the house?

How much interest have you paid the lender by the time you sell the house?
solution.html:
To calculate the monthly payment, we will use the following formula: \[ A = \frac{P \cdot i \cdot (1 + i)^n} {(1 + i)^n - 1} \] Here, the variables are defined as follows:
  • \( A \): Monthly payment
  • \( P \): Loan principal
  • \( i \): Monthly interest rate, calculated as \( i = \frac{r}{12} \)
  • \( n \): Total number of payments, calculated as \( n = \text{loanTerm} \times 12 \)
 First, calculate the monthly interest rate: \[ i = \frac{\frac{\text{annualInterestRate} }{100} }{12} \] Next, calculate the total number of payment periods: \[ n = \text{loanTerm} \times 12 \] Substitute the values of \( P \), \( i \), and \( n \) into the formula to calculate the monthly payment: \[ A = \frac{P \cdot i \cdot (1 + i)^n}{(1 + i)^n - 1} = \frac{ {{params.P}} \cdot {{params.im}} \cdot (1 + {{params.im}})^{360} }{(1 + {{params.im}})^{360} - 1} = {{params.A}}\] To calculate the remaining balance after \( k \) payments, we use the following formula: \[ B_k = A \cdot \frac{(1 + i)^{360-t} } {(1 + i)^{360-t} - 1} = {{params.A}} \cdot \frac{(1 + {{params.im}})^{360-{{params.t}} } } {(1 + {{params.im}})^{360-{{params.t}} } - 1} = {{correct_answers.amountOwed}} \] Here, the variables are defined as follows:
  • \( B_k \): Remaining balance after \( k \) payments
  • \( t \): Number of payments made
 To find the total amount paid by the lender, use the formula: \[ \text{Total Paid} = A \cdot t = {{params.A}} \cdot {{params.t}} = {{correct_answers.AmountPayed}}\] To find the principal paid, subtract the remaining balance from the loan amount: \[ \text{Principal Paid} = P - B_k = {{params.P}} - {{correct_answers.amountOwed}} = {{correct_answers.PrincipalPayed}}\] Finally, to calculate the interest paid, subtract the principal paid from the total amount paid: \[ \text{Interest Paid} = \text{Total Paid} - \text{Principal Paid} = {{correct_answers.AmountPayed}} - {{correct_answers.PrincipalPayed}} = {{correct_answers.IntrestPayed}} \]

question.html:
Compute the missing force vector that will allow for static equilibrium.

Provide the Magnitude of the force and the unit vector of the missing force vector.

Let the known forces be $\mathbf{F}_R = {{params.fr}} {{params.unitsForce}}$, $\mathbf{F}_O = {{params.fo}} {{params.unitsForce}}$, $\mathbf{F}_P = {{params.fp}} {{params.unitsForce}}$, and $\mathbf{F}_B = {{params.fb}} {{params.unitsForce}}$.

And let the lengths be $\mathbf{L}_1 = {{params.l1}} {{params.unitsDist}}$, $\mathbf{L}_2 = {{params.l2}} {{params.unitsDist}}$, and $\mathbf{L}_3 = {{params.l3}} {{params.unitsDist}}$.
solution.html:
The first step is to set convert all of the forces into forces vectors.This can be done by multiplying the force magnitude by the unit vector that follows the path of the force. To compute the unit vector all you have to due is divide the length of the vector by its self.
    Computing the Force vectors:
  • $\vec{F}_O = (F_O)(\vec{U}_O)$. let the unit vector $\vec{U}_O = \frac{-L_3\hat{i}-L_1\hat{j}+L_1\hat{k}}{\sqrt{(L_3)^2+(L_1)^2+(L_1)^2}}$

    • So the force vector $\vec{F}_O = (F_O)\frac{-L_3\hat{i}-L_1\hat{j}+L_1\hat{k}}{\sqrt{(L_3)^2+(L_1)^2+(L_1)^2}}$.

  • $\vec{F}_P = (F_P)(\vec{U}_P)$. let the unit vector $\vec{U}_P = \frac{-L_2\hat{i}+L_2\hat{j}+0\hat{k}}{\sqrt{(L_2)^2+(L_2)^2}}$ .

    • So the force vector $\vec{F}_P = (F_P) \frac{-L_2\hat{i}+L_2\hat{j}+0\hat{k}}{\sqrt{(L_2)^2+(L_2)^2}}$.

  • $\vec{F}_B = (F_B)(\vec{U}_B)$. let the unit vector $\vec{U}_B = \frac{L_2\hat{i}+L_1\hat{j}+L_2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{(L_2)^2+(L_2)^2+(L_1)^2}}$ .

    • So the force vector $\vec{F}_B = (F_B) \frac{L_2\hat{i}+L_1\hat{j}+L_2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{(L_2)^2+(L_2)^2+(L_1)^2}}$

  • $\vec{F}_R = (F_R)(\vec{U}_R)$. let the unit vector $\vec{U}_R = \frac{L_2\hat{i}-L_2\hat{j}-L_3\hat{k}}{\sqrt{(L_2)^2+(L_2)^2+(L_3)^2}}$ .

    • So the force vector $\vec{F}_R = (F_R) \frac{L_2\hat{i}-L_2\hat{j}-L_3\hat{k}}{\sqrt{(L_2)^2+(L_2)^2+(L_3)^2}}$

  • Now that you have all of the force vectors, set up the static equilibrium force equations.
    Setting up static equilibrium force equations:
  • $\Sigma{F}_x= 0 \implies -\vec{F}_O\hat{i}-\vec{F}_P\hat{i}+\vec{F}_B\hat{i}+\vec{F}_R\hat{i}+\vec{F}\hat{i} = 0$
  • $\Sigma{F}_y= 0 \implies -\vec{F}_O\hat{j}+\vec{F}_P\hat{j}+\vec{F}_B\hat{j}-\vec{F}_R\hat{j}+\vec{F}\hat{j} = 0$
  • $\Sigma{F}_z= 0 \implies \vec{F}_O\hat{z}+\vec{F}_B\hat{z}-\vec{F}_R\hat{z}+\vec{F}\hat{z} = 0$

    • Where $\vec{F}$ is the messing vector we want to find.

    Solving each equation for $\vec{F}\hat{i}$,$\vec{F}\hat{j}$, and $\vec{F}\hat{k}$

  • $\vec{F}\hat{i} = \vec{F}_O\hat{i}+\vec{F}_P\hat{i}-\vec{F}_B\hat{i}-\vec{F}_R\hat{i}$
  • $\vec{F}\hat{j} = \vec{F}_O\hat{j}+\vec{F}_R-\vec{F}_P\hat{j}\hat{j}-\vec{F}_B\hat{j}$
  • $\vec{F}\hat{k} = -\vec{F}_O\hat{k}-\vec{F}_B\hat{k}+\vec{F}_F\hat{k}$
    • Now that you have the missing vector, compute the magnitude and the unit vector.
    Computing magnitude:
  • $F = \sqrt{\vec{F}\hat{i}^2+\vec{F}\hat{j}^2+\vec{F}\hat{k}^2} = {{correct_answers.F}} {{params.unitsForce}}$.
    • Computing unit vector:
  • $\vec{U}_F = \frac{\vec{F}\hat{i}+\vec{F}\hat{j}+\vec{F}\hat{k}}{\sqrt{(\vec{F}\hat{i})^2+(\vec{F}\hat{j})^2+(\vec{F}\hat{k})^2}}$
  • $\vec{U}_F \hat{i} = {{correct_answers.Ufx}}$
  • $\vec{U}_F \hat{j} = {{correct_answers.Ufy}}$
  • $\vec{U}_F \hat{k} = {{correct_answers.Ufz}}$

First compute the reaction forces at points A and D by $ \Sigma F_x = 0 $, $ \Sigma F_y = 0 $ and $ \Sigma M_A = 0 $ of the whole system. Break up the system into 4 seprate parts. Beam AD,BF,CE, and pully F, and right the X and Y reaction forces acting at each point on all 4 parts.
    Solving reaction forces:
  • $ \Sigma F_x = 0, \implies A_x + D_x = 0, \implies A_x = -D_x$
  • $ \Sigma F_y = 0, \implies A_y - W = 0, \implies A_y = W, \implies A_y = {{params.W}} {{params.unitsForce}}$
  • $ \Sigma M_A = 0, \implies (D_x)(L_1+L_2+L_3+L_4) - (W)(L_1+L_2+r) = 0.$ Solving for $D_x = (W)(L_1+L_2+r) / (L_1+L_2+L_3+L_4) = {{correct_answers.DX}}$ ${{params.unitsForce}}$
    Reminder: If 2 parts share 1 point then the reactions on each parts must be equal oppisite to each other.
  • Example: when writing the reaction forces on beam AD.
  • Point A $\implies$ 2 reaction forces pointing right and up, (positve x direction) and (positive y direction).
  • Point B $\implies$ 2 reaction forces pointing right and up, (positve x direction) and (positive y direction).
  • Point C $\implies$ 2 reaction forces pointing right and up, (positve x direction) and (positive y direction).
  • Point D $\implies$ 1 reaction forces pointing right and up, (positve x direction).
  • There will also be a tension force pointing to the right, (positive x direction)
    • -
  • Example: when writing the reaction forces on beam CE.
  • Point C $\implies$ 2 reaction forces pointing left and down, (negative x direction) and (negative y direction).
  • Point E $\implies$ 2 reaction forces pointing right and up, (positive x direction) and (positive y direction).
    • -
  • Example: when writing the reaction forces on beam BF.
  • Point B $\implies$ 2 reaction forces pointing left and down, (negative x direction) and (negative y direction).
  • Point E $\implies$ 2 reaction forces pointing left and down, (negative x direction) and (negative y direction).
  • Point F $\implies$ 2 reaction forces pointing left and down, (negative x direction) and (negative y direction).
    • -
  • Example: when writing the reaction forces on pully F.
  • Point F $\implies$ 2 reaction forces pointing right and up, (positive x direction) and (positive y direction).
  • There will also be a 2 tension forces pointing left and down.
    • -
  • Now that everything is set up you can now start solving each part by doing $ \Sigma F_x = 0 $, $ \Sigma F_y = 0 $ and $ \Sigma M_A = 0. $
    Solving reaction forces:
  • Beam BF: $ \Sigma M_B = 0 \implies -(E_y)(L_2) - (W)(L_2+L_3+r)=0 \implies |E_y| = (W)(L_2+L_3+r)/-l_2 = {{correct_answers.DX}}$ ${{params.unitsForce}}$
    • -
  • Beam CE: tan($\theta$) = (opp/adj) $\implies$ tan($\theta$) =$ (L_1/L_2) \implies \theta = $atan$(L_1/L_2)$
  • Now we can solve for $E_x$: tan($\theta$) = $ E_y/E_x \implies |E_x| = E_y /$ tan($\theta$) = ${{correct_answers.EY}}$ ${{params.unitsForce}}$
  • By $ \Sigma F_x = 0 $, $ \Sigma F_y = 0 $ we can come to the conclusion that $C_x = E_x$ and $C_y = E_y$
    • -
  • Pully F: $ \Sigma F_x = 0 $, $ \Sigma F_y = 0 $ we can come to the conclusion that $F_y = W $ and $ F_x = W $
    • -
  • Beam BF: Now that we have $F_x,F_y,E_x,E_y$ we can solve for the reactions at point B.
  • $ \Sigma F_x = 0 $, $ \Sigma F_y = 0 \implies B_x = E_x - F_x,$ and $ B_y = E_y - F_y$
  • $B_x = {{correct_answers.BX}}$ {{params.unitsForce}}
  • $B_y = {{correct_answers.BY}}$ {{params.unitsForce}}
    • -
  • Note: The solutions want the magnitude of the forces which is why they all come out positve.
  • When you get negative solutions for reaction forces, that indactes that you have to switch the force direction.
  • For example: This is why when solving for $B_x$ it NOT $B_x = E_x + F_x$ even though that is technically correct with the way we initially drew the forces.
  • It is beacuse the true direction of $E_x$ on beam BF is to the right (positive x direction) regardless of the direction of our initial guess.

question.html: You would like to purchase a house. You plan to make a down payment equal to {{params.down_payment_percent}}% of the purchase price and take out a {{params.mortgage_years}}-year, fixed-rate mortgage for the remaining {{params.mortgage_percent}}%. You would like to select a house such that your monthly payment, including mortgage and taxes, does not exceed {{params.monthly_payment}} USD. The annual tax rate is {{params.tax_rate}}% of the purchase price and there is a special assessment for the local school district of {{params.special_assessment}} USD per year. You can assume that 1/12th of the tax and assessment is paid each month. If the interest rate is {{params.interest_rate}}%/year compounded monthly, what is the most expensive house you can afford?
solution.html:
To find the maximum house price you can afford, we can break down the problem into several components. The down payment is calculated as a percentage of the purchase price, and the mortgage is based on the remaining amount after the down payment. The monthly payment should include both the mortgage payment and any taxes or assessments. The down payment can be expressed as:
\[ D = \frac{ {{params.down_payment_percent}} }{100} \times P \]
where \( D \) is the down payment, \( P \) is the purchase price, and \( {{params.down_payment_percent}} \) is the given percentage. The amount financed through the mortgage is:
\[ M = P - D = P - ( \frac{ {{params.down_payment_percent}} }{100} \times P ) = P ( 1 - \frac{ {{params.down_payment_percent}} }{100} ) \] The monthly mortgage payment can be calculated using the formula:
\[ PMT = \frac{M \cdot r (1 + r)^{n} }{(1 + r)^{n} - 1} \]
where \( r = \frac{ {{params.interest_rate}} }{100 \times 12} \) is the monthly interest rate, and \( n = {{params.mortgage_years}} \times 12 \) is the total number of payments. The total monthly payment including taxes and assessments is:
\[ Total Payment = PMT + \frac{ \frac{ {{params.tax_rate}} } {100} \times P + {{params.special_assessment}} } {12} \] Setting the total payment equal to the maximum monthly payment, we get:
\[ PMT + \frac{ \frac{ {{params.tax_rate}} } {100} \times P + {{params.special_assessment}} } {12} = {{params.monthly_payment}} \]
By substituting the expression for \( PMT \) into this equation, we can solve for \( P \). Solviing for P will give you the solution of: P = {{correct_answers.max_house_price}} USD.

solution.html:
The Present worth cvan be written as:

Pw = -(Initial Investment) + (Cash flow) + (Present given future)

  • Where the initial investment is {{params.investment}}

  • The cash flow is given as: ${{params.annualCashFlow}} \cdot \frac{(1+{{params.marr}})^{ {{params.annualYears}} }-1 } { {{params.marr}}(1 + {{params.marr}})^{ {{params.annualYears}} } }$

  • The Present given future can be written as: $\frac{ {{params.lumpsum}} }{ (1+ {{params.marr}} )^{ {{params.totalYears}} } }$
    •  Putting it all together we can obtain the present worth as:

    Pw = -{{params.investment}} + ${{params.annualCashFlow}} \cdot \frac{(1+{{params.marr}})^{ {{params.annualYears}} }-1 } { {{params.marr}}(1 + {{params.marr}})^{ {{params.annualYears}} } }$ + $\frac{ {{params.lumpsum}} }{ (1+ {{params.marr}} )^{ {{params.totalYears}} } }$ = {{correct_answers.presentWorth}} USD

    Using a nonlinear solver we can obtain IRR to be: IRR = {{correct_answers.irr}} %

To calculate the equivalent present worth (PW) of the cash flows, we can use the formula: \[ PW = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{R_t}{(1 + i)^t} \] where \( R_t \) is the net cash flow in year \( t \), \( i \) is the MARR, and \( n \) is the useful life of the asset. First, we need to determine the net cash flow for each year: \[ R_t = \text{Annual Income} - \text{Annual Expenses} \] Substitute the known variables: \[ R_t = {{params.annualIncome}} - {{params.annualExpenses}} \] Next, we will calculate the present worth for the income generated for each year over the lifespan of the band saw, excluding the salvage value, using the MARR: \[ PW_{income} = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{R_t}{(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^t} = ({{params.annualIncome}} - {{params.annualExpenses}}) \frac{(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^n -1}{ \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100}(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^n } \] and for the salvage value at the end of the lifespan: \[ PW_{salvage} = \frac{ {{params.salvageValue}} }{ {(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^{n} } } \] Finally, the total equivalent present worth is given by: \[ PW = -Cost PW_{income} + PW_{salvage} \] Substitute the values to calculate the final present worth: \[ PW =- {{params.cost}} + ({{params.annualIncome}} - {{params.annualExpenses}}) \frac{(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^n -1}{ \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100}(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^n } + \frac{ {{params.salvageValue}} }{ {(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^{n} } } \] Therefore, the equivalent present worth of the cash flows is \( PW = {{correct_answers.presentWorth}} ~{{params.unitsCost}} \). The annual worth is calculated in a simular way, using annual given present:

A = pw $\frac{i(1+i)^n}{(i+1)^n -1 }$

Plugging in we can solve for A:

\[ A = {{correct_answers.presentWorth}} \frac{ {{params.i}}(1+{{params.i}})^{7} }{(1+{{params.i}})^{7} -1 } = {{correct_answers.aw}}~ USD \]

 The future worth can be solved by bringing the present worth fowards in time: Fw = Pw$(1+i)^7$

Plugging in we can solve for the future worth to be:

\[Fw = {{correct_answers.presentWorth}} (1+{{params.i}})^7 = {{correct_answers.fw}} ~USD \]

 To solve for the internal rate of return (IRR) we have to set the present worth equal to zero and solve for i = irr.

\[ PW= 0 =- {{params.cost}} + ({{params.annualIncome}} - {{params.annualExpenses}}) \frac{(1 + IRR)^n -1}{ IRR(1 + IRR)^n } + \frac{ {{params.salvageValue}} }{ {(1 + IRR)^{n} } } \]

Using a nonlinear solver we can obtain IRR to be: IRR = {{correct_answers.irr}} %

question.html: A loan of {{params.loanAmount}} USD is to be paid off in {{params.numPayments}} equal annual payments. The interest rate is {{params.interestRate}}% per year compounded annually. If the first payment is made at the end of Year 0, what is the annual payment?
solution.html:
To find the annual payment for the loan, we can use the formula for the present value of an annuity, which is given by: $P = A + A \frac{(r+1)^{n-1} }{r(r+1)^{n-1} }$ where:
  • \( P \) is the present value of the loan (loan amount),
  • \( A \) is the annual payment,
  • \( r \) is the interest rate per period (annual interest rate), and
  • \( n \) is the total number of payments.
 Rearranging the formula to solve for the annual payment \( A \), we get: $A = \frac{P}{1+ \frac{(r+1)^{n-1} }{r(r+1)^{n-1} } }$ In this case, the values we need to substitute are:
  • \( P = {{params.loanAmount}} \text{ USD} \),
  • \( r = \frac{ {{params.interestRate}} } {100} \),
  • \( n = {{params.numPayments}} \).
 Substituting these values into the equation for \( A \), we have: $A = \frac{ {{params.loanAmount}} }{1+ \frac{(\frac{ {{params.interestRate}} } {100}+1)^{ {{params.numPayments}}-1} }{\frac{ {{params.interestRate}} } {100}(\frac{ {{params.interestRate}} } {100}+1)^{ {{params.numPayments}}-1} } }$ This gives us the annual payment amount of \( {{correct_answers.annualPayment}} \text{ USD} \).

question.html: Washington Mill Works is considering the purchase of a large resawing band saw for {{params.cost}} USD . The saw is expected to have a useful life of {{params.lifespan}} {{params.unitsYears}}, after which it will have an estimated salvage value of ${{params.salvageValue}} {{params.unitsCost}}. Each year, the annual income is estimated to be {{params.annualIncome}} {{params.unitsIncome}}, while the annual operating expenses are {{params.annualExpenses}} {{params.unitsExpenses}}. Assuming a minimum attractive rate of return (MARR) of {{params.MARR}}%, calculate the equivalent present worth of the cash flows over the seven-year period.
solution.html:
<pl-solution-panel>
    <pl-hint level="1" data-type="text">
        To calculate the equivalent present worth (PW) of the cash flows, we can use the formula: 
        \[ PW = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{R_t}{(1 + i)^t} \]
        where \( R_t \) is the net cash flow in year \( t \), \( i \) is the MARR, and \( n \) is the useful life of the asset.
    </pl-hint>
    <pl-hint level="2" data-type="text">
        First, we need to determine the net cash flow for each year: 
        \[ R_t = \text{Annual Income} - \text{Annual Expenses} \] 
        Substitute the known variables: 
        \[ R_t = {{params.annualIncome}} - {{params.annualExpenses}} \]
    </pl-hint>
    <pl-hint level="3" data-type="text">
        Next, we will calculate the present worth for the income generated for each year over the lifespan of the band saw, excluding the salvage value, using the MARR: 
        \[ PW_{income} = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{R_t}{(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^t}  = ({{params.annualIncome}} - {{params.annualExpenses}}) \frac{(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^n -1}{ \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100}(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^n  } \] 
        and for the salvage value at the end of the lifespan: 
        \[ PW_{salvage} = \frac{ {{params.salvageValue}} }{ {(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^{n} } } \] 
    </pl-hint>
    <pl-hint level="4" data-type="text">
        Finally, the total equivalent present worth is given by: 
        \[ PW = -Cost PW_{income} + PW_{salvage} \] 
        Substitute the values to calculate the final present worth: 
        \[ PW =- {{params.cost}} + ({{params.annualIncome}} - {{params.annualExpenses}}) \frac{(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^n -1}{ \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100}(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^n  } + \frac{ {{params.salvageValue}} }{ {(1 + \frac{ {{params.MARR}} }{100})^{n} } } \]
    </pl-hint>
    <pl-hint level="5" data-type="text">
        Therefore, the equivalent present worth of the cash flows is \( PW = {{correct_answers.presentWorth}} ~{{params.unitsCost}} \).
    </pl-hint>
</pl-solution-panel>

question.html: How much should be deposited at t = {{params.t0}} into a fund paying {{params.rate}} compounded per period in order to withdraw {{params.withdraw1}}$ at t = {{params.t1}}, {{params.withdraw2}} at t = {{params.t2}}, and {{params.withdraw3}} at t = {{params.t3}} such that the fund is depleted at the last withdrawal?
solution.html:
To determine the amount that should be deposited at time \( t_0 \) into the fund, we need to calculate the present value of each withdrawal and sum these values. The present value of each withdrawal can be calculated using the formula: \[ PV = \frac{FV}{(1 + r)^n} \] where \( FV \) is the future value (withdrawal amount), \( r \) is the interest rate per period, and \( n \) is the number of periods until the withdrawal. For the three withdrawals, we calculate: Here $t_0 = 0$
  • For the first withdrawal of \( \ {{params.withdraw1}} \) at time \( t_1 \): \[ PV_1 = \frac{ {{params.withdraw1}} }{(1 + {{params.rate}})^{t_1 - t_0} } \]
  • For the second withdrawal of \( \ {{params.withdraw2}} \) at time \( t_2 \): \[ PV_2 = \frac{ {{params.withdraw2}} }{(1 + {{params.rate}})^{t_2 - t_0} } \]
  • For the third withdrawal of \( \ {{params.withdraw3}} \) at time \( t_3 \): \[ PV_3 = \frac{ {{params.withdraw3}} }{(1 + {{params.rate}})^{t_3 - t_0} } \]
 The total present value (deposit amount) required at time \( t_0 \) is the sum of the present values of all withdrawals: \[ Deposit = PV_1 + PV_2 + PV_3 \] Substituting the values gives us the required deposit amount to ensure the fund is depleted at the last withdrawal: \[ Deposit = \frac{ {{params.withdraw1}} }{(1 + {{params.rate}})^{t_1 - t_0} } + \frac{ {{params.withdraw2}} }{(1 + {{params.rate}})^{t_2 - t_0} } + \frac{ {{params.withdraw3}} } {(1 + {{params.rate}})^{t_3 - t_0} } \]

First solve for the monthly payment using the equation:

  • A = loan amount $\frac{i(1+i)^n}{(i+1)^n -1 }$

  • A = ${{params.loan}} \frac{ {{params.i}}(1+{{params.i}})^5}{ (1+{{params.i}})^5 -1 } = {{params.A}}$
    •

    BTLCF (Before-Tax-and-Loan Cash Flow):

  • This is the given revenue minus cost, which is constant at {{params.BTLCF}} each year.

    MACRS Deduction:

  • Year 1: 33.33%
  • Year 2: 44.45%
  • Year 3: 14.81%
  • Year 4: 7.41%
  • Year 5: 0% (fully depreciated).

    • MACRS Deduction = (Machine Cost) $\times$ (MACRS Percentage)

    Book Value:

  • Subtract the cumulative MACRS deductions from the machine's purchase price {{params.cost}}. This tracks the remaining depreciation value of the machine:
  • Book Value at t= (Book value at t-1) - (depreciation at t)
    •

  • Multiply the remaining loan principal at the start of the year by the annual interest rate {{params.rate}}%.

  • Subtract the loan interest payment from the total fixed annual loan payment {{params.A}}.
  • The principal payment increases each year as the interest decreases.

    • Principal Payment = Total Payment - Loan Interest Payment

    Remaining Principal:

from numpy.polynomial import Polynomial
from numpy.polynomial.polynomial import polyval
import numpy as np
from pytexit import py2tex

def poly(p, var_string='x'):
    res = ''
    first_pow = len(p) - 1
    for i, coef in enumerate(p):
        power = first_pow - i

        if coef:
            if coef < 0:
                sign, coef = (' - ' if res else '- '), -coef
            elif coef > 0: # must be true
                sign = (' + ' if res else '')

            str_coef = '' if coef == 1 and power != 0 else str(coef)

            if power == 0:
                str_power = ''
            elif power == 1:
                str_power = var_string
            else:
                str_power = var_string + '^' + str(power)

            res += sign + str_coef + str_power 
    return res

def bisection(p, xl, xu, errTol):
    curErr = 100000000
    xmold = xl
    
    ix = 0
    ca = []
    numIter = 6
    while curErr > errTol and ix <= numIter:
        xm = (xl + xu)/2
        fxl = polyval(xl, p.coef)
        fxm = polyval(xm, p.coef)
        fxu = polyval(xu, p.coef)

        if fxl*fxm < 0:
            xu = xm
        else:
            xl = xm
        
        curErr = abs((xm-xmold)/xm)
        xmold = xm
        # print('XM is ', xm,' and current Error is ', curErr)
        step = {'stepNum': ix,
                'xl': xl,
                'xu': xu,
                'fxl': fxl,
                'fxm': fxm,
                'fxu': fxu,
                'curErr': curErr}
        ix = ix + 1 
        ca.append(step)

question.html:
Air enters the compressor of a gas turbine at a pressure of ${{params.Pressure1}}$ ${{params.unitsPressure}}$ and at a temperature of ${{params.T1}}$${{params.unitsTemperature}}$ .

The pressure ratio is {{params.pr}} and the maximum temperature is ${{params.T3}} {{params.unitsTemperature}}$.

Using the Brayton cycle, Determine the back work ratio and the thermal efficiency. (Assume k = 1.4)
solution.html:
The back work ratio can be found using the following formula: BWR = $\frac{ W_{comp} }{ W_{turb} }$ = $\frac{c_p*(T_2 - T_1)}{c_p*(T_3 - T_4)}$ The Brayton cyle utilizes isentropic compression and expansion.
  • $T_2$ = $T_1$*$(\frac{P_2}{P_1})^\frac{k-1}{k}$ = {{params.T1S}} * $({{params.pr}})^\frac{1.4-1}{1.4}$ = {{params.T2}}${{params.unitsTemperatures}}$
  • $T_4$ = $T_3$*$(\frac{P_4}{P_3})^\frac{k-1}{k}$ = {{params.T3S}} * $(\frac{1}{ {{params.pr}} })^\frac{1.4-1}{1.4}$ = {{params.T4}}${{params.unitsTemperatures}}$
BWR = $\frac{T_2 - T_1}{T_3 - T_4}$ = $\frac{ {{params.T2}} - {{params.T1S}} }{ {{params.T3S}} - {{params.T4}} }$ = {{correct_answers.BWR}}%. The thermal efficiency is $η$ = 1 - $(r)^\frac{1-k}{k}$ = 1 - $({{params.pr}})^\frac{1-1.4}{1.4}$ = {{correct_answers.Eff}}%.
title: Brayton Cycle

question.html:
Air enters the compressor of a gas turbine at a pressure of ${{params.Pressure1}}$ ${{params.unitsPressure}}$ and at a temperature of ${{params.T1}}$${{params.unitsTemperature}}$ .

The pressure ratio is {{params.pr}} and the maximum temperature is ${{params.T3}} {{params.unitsTemperature}}$.

The compressor and turbine efficiencies are {{params.E1Old}}% and {{params.E2Old}}%.

Using the Brayton cycle, Determine the back work ratio and the thermal efficiency. (Assume k = 1.4)
solution.html:
To determine the back work ratio and the thermal efficiency we must find $w_{comp}$, $w_{turb}$, and $q_{in}$.
  • The compressor work: $w_{comp}$ = $\frac{ w_{comp,s} }{ η_{comp} }$ = $\frac{c_p*(T_{2,s} - T_1)}{ η_{comp} }$ (where $T_{2,s}$ is the temperature at state 2 assuming an isentropic process).
  • similarly, the turbine work: $w_{turb}$ = ($η_{turb}$)*($w_{turb,s}$) = ($η_{turb}$)*$c_p$*($T_3$ - $T_{4,s}$) (where $T_{4,s}$ is the temperature at state 4 assuming an isentropic process)
  • $T_{2,s}$ = $T_1$*$(\frac{P_2}{P_1})^\frac{k-1}{k}$ = {{params.T1S}} * $({{params.pr}})^\frac{1.4-1}{1.4}$ = {{params.T2S}}${{params.unitsTemperatures}}$
  • $T_{4,s}$ = $T_3$*$(\frac{P_4}{P_3})^\frac{k-1}{k}$ = {{params.T3S}} * $(\frac{1}{ {{params.pr}} })^\frac{1.4-1}{1.4}$ = {{params.T4S}}${{params.unitsTemperatures}}$
  • $w_{comp}$ = $\frac{ {{params.cp}}*({{params.T2S}} - {{params.T1S}}) }{ {{params.E1}} }$ = {{params.Wc}} ${{params.unitsSpecificEnthalpy}}$
  • $w_{turb}$ = ({{params.E2}})*${{params.cp}}$*(${{params.T3S}}$ - ${{params.T4S}}$) = {{params.Wt}} ${{params.unitsSpecificEnthalpy}}$
  • The back work ratio is then: BWR = $\frac{ w_{comp} }{ w_{turb} }$ = {{correct_answers.BWR}}%.
  • The heat transfer input in this cycle is $q_{in}$ = $h_3$ - $h_2$ = $c_p$*($T_3$ - $T_2$). (where $T_2$ is the actual temperature)
  • $T_2$ can be found using the $w_{comp}$ equation: $T_2$ = $\frac{ w_{comp} }{c_p}$ + $T_1$ = {{params.T2}}{{params.unitsTemperatures}}.
  • $q_{in}$ = {{params.Qin}} ${{params.unitsSpecificEnthalpy}}$
 The thermal efficiency can then be written as: $η$ = $\frac{ w_{net} }{ q{in} }$ = $\frac{ w_{turb} - w_{comp} }{ q{in} }$ = {{correct_answers.Eff}}%.

solution.html:
Steps to solving Double Decline Depreciation with Switch to Straight-Line

$ \textbf{1. Depreciation Rate:}$ \[ \text{Depreciation Rate} = \frac{2}{\text{Useful Life (in years)} } \] $\textbf{2. Depreciation Expense for Each Year:}$ \[ \text{Depreciation Expense (Year n)} = \text{Book Value at Beginning of Year n} \times \text{Depreciation Rate} \] $ \textbf{3. Book Value for Each Year:}$ \[ \text{Book Value (Year n)} = \text{Book Value at Beginning of Year (n-1)} - \text{Depreciation Expense (Year n)} \] $\textbf{4. Ensure Book Value Does Not Fall Below Salvage Value:}$ \[ \text{If Book Value (Year n)} < \text{Salvage Value, then Book Value (Year n)} = \text{Salvage Value} \] $\textbf{5. Switch to Straight-Line Depreciation:}$ \[ \text{Straight-Line Depreciation} = \frac{\text{Book Value at Start of Year} - \text{Salvage Value} }{\text{Remaining Life} } \] \[ \text{Switch to Straight-Line Depreciation when:} \] \[ \text{Stright Line depreciation > Double decline depreciation} \] The initial book value at the end of year 0 (EOY 0) is equal to the purchase price: {{params.purchase_price}}.   • Green distributed load into a concentrated force: $F_G$ = integral from 0 to ${{params.length1}}$ of w(x) = $(({{params.constant}})({{params.length2}})^3)/3.$

solution.html:
Steps to solving Double Decline

$ \textbf{1. Depreciation Rate:}$ \[ \text{Depreciation Rate} = \frac{2}{\text{Useful Life (in years)} } \] $\textbf{2. Depreciation Expense for Each Year:}$ \[ \text{Depreciation Expense (Year n)} = \text{Book Value at Beginning of Year n} \times \text{Depreciation Rate} \] $ \textbf{3. Book Value for Each Year:}$ \[ \text{Book Value (Year n)} = \text{Book Value at Beginning of Year (n-1)} - \text{Depreciation Expense (Year n)} \] $\textbf{4. Ensure Book Value Does Not Fall Below Salvage Value:}$ \[ \text{If Book Value (Year n)} < \text{Salvage Value, then Book Value (Year n)} = \text{Salvage Value} \] The initial book value at the end of year 0 (EOY 0) is equal to the purchase price: {{params.purchase_price}}. question.html:
Air enters the compressor of an Ericsson cycle at a pressure of ${{params.Pressure1S}}$ ${{params.unitsPressure}}$ and at a temperature of ${{params.T1}}$${{params.unitsTemperature}}$ .

The pressure ratio is {{params.pr}} and the maximum temperature is ${{params.T3}} {{params.unitsTemperature}}$.

Determine the work output and the heat input.
solution.html:
To determine the work output for the Ericsson cycle, we must find the work for each process: $W_{out}$ = $W_{1-2}$ + $W_{2-3}$ + $W_{3-4}$ + $W_{4-1}$.
  • For process 1-2: since it is an isothermal process, $W_{1-2}$ = R*$T_1$*ln($\frac{v_2}{v_1}$).
  • For process 2-3: since it is an isobaric process, $W_{2-3}$ = $P_2$*($v_3$ - $v_2$).
  • For process 3-4: since it is an isothermal process, $W_{3-4}$ = R*$T_3$*ln($\frac{v_4}{v_3}$).
  • For process 4-1: since it is an isobaric process, $W_{4-1}$ = $P_1$*($v_1$ - $v_4$).
  • We must now calculate the unknowns ($P_2$,$v_1$,$v_2$,$v_3$,$v_4$).
  • Using the ideal gas law, $v_1$ = $\frac{R*T_1}{P_1}$ = {{params.v1}}${{params.unitsSpecificVolume}}$. (make any necessary conversions)
  • For the isobaric process 4-1, $\frac{T_4}{v_4}$ = $\frac{T_1}{v_1}$ $\implies$ $v_4$ = $\frac{T_4}{T_1}$ * $v_1$ = {{params.v4}}${{params.unitsSpecificVolume}}$.
  • From the definition of the compression ratio, $\frac{v_4}{v_2}$ = {{params.pr}} $\implies$ $v_2$ = $\frac{v_4}{ {{params.pr}} }$ = {{params.v2}}${{params.unitsSpecificVolume}}$.
  • Using the ideal gas law, $P_2$ = $\frac{R*T_2}{v_2}$ = {{params.Pressure2}}{{params.unitsPressures}}.
  • $v_3$ can now be solved since $P_2$ = $P_3$: $v_3$ = $\frac{R*T_3}{P_3}$ = {{params.v3}}${{params.unitsSpecificVolume}}$.
Making any necessary conversions and plugging in all the values, $W_{output}$ = {{correct_answers.Work}}{{params.unitsSpecificEnthalpy}}.
  • Finally, the thermal efficiency is: $η$ = 1 - $\frac{ T_{Low} }{ T_{High} }$ = {{params.Eff}}.
  • $q_{in}$ = $\frac{ W_{output} }{η}$ = {{correct_answers.Qin}}{{params.unitsSpecificEnthalpy}}.

def forwardElimination(C):
    (nRows, nCols) = C.shape

    C = C.astype('float32')
   # print(C.dtype)
    #print('nRows = ', nRows, ' nCols = ', nCols)
    status = False

    for i in range(0, nRows):
        pivot = C[i,i]
        
        if abs(pivot) < 1e-5:
     #       print('Pivot is zero: Need new matrix')
            return (status, C, ca)
    
        for k in range(i+1, nRows):
            fac = C[k,i]/pivot
      #      print('Factor = ', fac)
            C[k,:] = C[k,:] - fac*C[i,:]
       #     print('During elimination = ', C)
            step = { 'stepNum': i, 'A': C[:, 0:nRows-1].tolist(), 'b': C[:, nRows].tolist()}
            ca.append(step)

    status = True
    # print('After Elimination = ', C)
    return (status, C, ca)

def backSubstitution(C):
    (nRows, nCols) = C.shape
    sol = np.zeros((nRows,1))

For the payday loan problem, what is the effective annual interest rate? Don't be shocked â€” the answer is big.
solution.html:
The interest rate for a loan can be calculated using the formula for compound interest: \[ A = P(1 + r)^n \] where \( A \) is the amount of money accumulated after n periods, \( P \) is the principal amount (the initial loan), \( i \) is the interest rate, and \( n \) is the number of periods. In this case, we can rearrange the formula to solve for the interest rate \( r \): \[ i = \left( \frac{A}{P} \right)^{\frac{1}{n} } - 1 \] Substitute the given values into the formula: \[ i = ( \frac{ {{params.repaymentAmount}} }{ {{params.loanAmount}} })^{\frac{1}{ {{params.time}} } } - 1 \] The interest rate for the loan is therefore: \[ i = {{correct_answers.interestRate}} \% \] To solve for the ammount owed after {{params.n}} weeks, all we have to do is solve the Future given present equation:

$F = P (i + 1)^n$

Where

  • F = Future worth
  • i = interest Rate = {{correct_answers.interestRate}}
  • n = number of payment periods missed = {{params.n}}

    • P = principle

    Solving we get: F = ${{params.loanAmount}} \cdot (1+{{params.i}})^{ {{params.n}} }$

    F = {{correct_answers.owed}} USD     To solve for the effect annual intrest rate, we can use this equation: $I_{eff} = (1+i)^w -1$

    Where:

  • i = The 2 week interest rate = {{params.i}}
  • w = time scaling facter = $52/2$
    • There are 52 weeks in 1 year, and the interest we calculated is compunded every two weeks. For example, if the interest was compouned every 4 weeks then w = 52/4.

    Solving we get: $I_{eff} = (1+{{params.i}})^{ {{params.w}} } -1$ = {{correct_answers.Ieff}} %

solution.html:
The partial pressure ($P_v$) of water vapor can be found using the formula: $P_v$ = $P_g$ * $ϕ$ = {{params.Pg}} * {{params.RH}} = {{params.Pv}} {{params.unitsPressure}}, where $P_g$ is the saturation pressure at {{params.OldT1}}{{params.unitsTemperature}} found in the steam tables.
  • The partial pressure of air is then $P_a$ = $P$ - $P_v$ = {{params.Pressure1}} - {{params.Pv}} = {{params.Pa}} {{params.unitsPressure}}.
  • The humidity ratio is then $ω$ = 0.622*$\frac{P_v}{P_a}$ = {{correct_answers.HR}} {{params.unitsMassRatio}}.
 The humidity ratio by definition is $ω$ = $\frac{m_v}{m_a}$. Using the ideal gas equation, $m_a$ = $\frac{P_a*V}{R_a*T}$. After making any necessary conversions, $m_v$ = $ω$ * $m_a$ = {{correct_answers.Mv}} {{params.unitsMass}}s.

You can use Proof Blocks by using a pl-order-blocks element with grading-method="dag". Use the depends attribute on each line is to denote which lines of the proof must appear before that line. The autograder will use this dependency information to construct the dependency graph of the proof. Then a correct answer is a topological sort of the lines of the proof. This example also uses the option feedback="first-wrong" to give the student feedback about where the first wrong line of their proof was.

Example 1: Use a proof by contrapositive to show that if $2m^2 + n + 1$ is even then either $m$ or $n$ are odd.

Proof by Contrapositive: Take some $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ Take some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ Assume $m$ is even Assume $n$ is even $\exists l \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $m = 2l$ $\exists k \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $n = 2k$ $2m^2 + n + 1 = 2(2l)^2 + 2k + 1 = 2(4l^2 + k) + 1$ Then since $2(4l^2 + k)$ is even, $2(4l^2 + k) + 1$ is odd.

Example 2:Let $A, B,$ and $C$ be propositions. Prove that $(A \land C) \lor (A \land B) \rightarrow A $

This example uses the pl-block-group element, which can be used to divide a proof into cases. In a proof that has cases, a correct answer is any topological sort of the lines, with the added condition that any lines in the same pl-block-group element must appear contiguously in the solution, as when you are writing a proof by cases, you finish one case before proving the next case.

Proof by Cases: Case $A \land C$: Since $A \land C$ is true, we know $A$ is true. Case $A \land B$: Since $A \land B$ is true, we know $A$ is true. This completes the proof.

import prairielearn as pl


def generate(data):
    # Dimensions
    nInnerMin = 2
    nMax = 5
    nRows = np.random.randint(1, nMax + 1)
    nInner = np.random.randint(nInnerMin, nMax + 1)
    nCols = np.random.randint(1, nMax + 1)

    # Number of digits after the decimal
    nDigits = 1

    # Range of entries
    numMax = 10

    # The two matrices to be multiplied
    Are = np.random.random_integers(-numMax, numMax, (nRows, nInner)) / (10**nDigits)
    Aim = np.random.random_integers(-numMax, numMax, (nRows, nInner)) / (10**nDigits)
    Bre = np.random.random_integers(-numMax, numMax, (nInner, nCols)) / (10**nDigits)
    Bim = np.random.random_integers(-numMax, numMax, (nInner, nCols)) / (10**nDigits)

    data["params"]["A"] = pl.to_json(A)
    data["params"]["B"] = pl.to_json(B)
    data["correct_answers"]["C"] = pl.to_json(C)

        if fmax - fmin > 12:
            plt.yticks([y for y in range(fmin, fmax + 4, 4)], fontsize=14)
            plt.gca().set_yticks([y for y in range(fmin, fmax + 1, 1)], minor=True)

            plt.yticks([y for y in range(fmin, fmax + 1, 1)], fontsize=14)

        plt.ylabel("$f(x)$", fontsize=18)
        plt.autoscale(enable=True, tight=True)
        fig.set_tight_layout(True)

        plt.savefig(buf, format="png")

def poly(p, var_string='x'):
    res = ''
    first_pow = len(p) - 1
    for i, coef in enumerate(p):
        power = first_pow - i

        if coef:
            if coef < 0:
                sign, coef = (' - ' if res else '- '), -coef
            elif coef > 0: # must be true
                sign = (' + ' if res else '')

            str_coef = '' if coef == 1 and power != 0 else str(coef)

            if power == 0:
                str_power = ''
            elif power == 1:
                str_power = var_string
            else:
                str_power = var_string + '^' + str(power)

            res += sign + str_coef + str_power 
    return res

{{params.Mass}} ${{params.unitsMass}}$ of air fills the cylinder of a piston-cylinder assembly. The initial volume and pressure are ${{params.Volume1}} {{params.unitsVolume}}$ and ${{params.Pressure1}} {{params.unitsPressure}}$.

At constant pressure, heat transfer to the air occurs until the volume is doubled. Kinetic and potential energy effects are negligible.

If the specific heat is constant, $c_v$ = ${{params.Cv}} {{params.unitsCv}}$, and the specific gas constant R = ${{params.Rs}} {{params.unitsRs}} $.

Calculate the heat transfer for the process.
solution.html:
Write the energy balance for this problem. The energy balance can be written as: △KE + △PE + △U = Q - W. This then can be reduced to: Q = △U + W. Expand "△U" and "W" using the correct assumptions for this problem.
  • The change of internal energy can be expressed as: △U = m*($U_2$ - $U_1$) = m*$c_v$*($T_2$ - $T_1$).
  • At constant pressure, Work can be expressed as: W = $\int_{V_1}^{V_2}PdV$ = P*($V_2$ - $V_1$).
  • The heat transfer for this process can now be written as: Q = m*$c_v$*($T_2$ - $T_1$) + P*($V_2$ - $V_1$).
  • To evalute $T_1$, we need to use the ideal gas equation: $P_1$*$V_1$ = m*R*$T_1$ $\implies$ $T_1$ = $\frac{P_1*V_1}{m*R}$ = {{params.T1}}{{params.unitsTemperature}}
  • Since $P_1$ = $P_2$, $\frac{m*R*T_1}{V_1}$ = $\frac{m*R*T_2}{V_2}$ $\implies$ $T_2$ = $\frac{V_2}{V_1}$*$T_1$ = {{params.T2}}{{params.unitsTemperature}}
Plug all values in to get: Q = {{correct_answers.Q}} ${{params.unitsHeat}}$

    <pl-hint level="3" data-type="text">
        The height of the plane at the time the object hits the ground is calculated using \( h = {params.H} + {params.vy} \times {params.t} + \frac{1}{2} \times {params.a} \times {params.t}^2 \), where \( a \) is the plane's acceleration in {params.unitsAcc}.

question.html: A car traveling at an initial speed of {{params.v}} {{params.unitsSpeed}} accelerates at {{params.a}} {{params.unitsAcceleration}}. How far (in {{params.unitsDist}}) does it travel in the third second after it begins to accelerate?
solution.html:
<pl-solution-panel>
    <pl-hint level="1" data-type="text">
        To calculate the distance traveled in the third second, we first find the total distance traveled in the first three seconds and then subtract the distance traveled in the first two seconds.
    </pl-hint>
    <pl-hint level="2" data-type="text">
        The total distance traveled in the first three seconds can be calculated using the kinematic equation: \( \Delta x_3 = v_0 \times 3 + \frac{1}{2} \times a \times 3^2 \), where \( v_0 \) is the initial speed and \( a \) is the acceleration.
    </pl-hint>
    <pl-hint level="3" data-type="text">
        Similarly, the distance for the first two seconds is calculated as: \( \Delta x_2 = v_0 \times 2 + \frac{1}{2} \times a \times 2^2 \).
    </pl-hint>
    <pl-hint level="4" data-type="text">
        The distance traveled during the third second is then \( \Delta x_3 - \Delta x_2 \).
    </pl-hint>
    <pl-hint level="5" data-type="text">
        Substituting \( v_0 = {params.v} {params.unitsSpeed} \) and \( a = {params.a} {params.unitsAcceleration} \) gives the distance traveled in the third second as \( {correct_answers.d} {params.unitsDist} \).
    </pl-hint>
</pl-solution-panel>

The remaining time (in minutes) in which the cyclist needs to complete the race to beat this record is:
solution.html:
<pl-solution-panel>
<pl-hint level="1" data-type="text">
The total distance of the race is {params.d} {params.unitsDist}, and the cyclist has already covered {params.d1} {params.unitsDist} in {params.t1} {params.unitsTime}.
</pl-hint>
<pl-hint level="2" data-type="text">
The remaining distance to be covered is {params.d} - {params.d1} {params.unitsDist}.
</pl-hint>
<pl-hint level="3" data-type="text">
The record speed is {params.vr} {params.unitsSpeed}. The time taken to cover a distance at a given speed is given by the formula \(t = \frac{d}{v}\).
</pl-hint>
<pl-hint level="4" data-type="text">
Therefore, the time needed to cover the remaining distance at the record speed is \(t = \frac{({params.d} - {params.d1})}{params.vr}\).
</pl-hint>
<pl-hint level="5" data-type="text">
The cyclist has already spent {params.t1} {params.unitsTime} on the first part of the race. To beat the record, the total time spent must be less than the record time. Therefore, the remaining time in which the cyclist needs to complete the race is \(t = \frac{({params.d} - {params.d1})}{params.vr} - {params.t1}\) {params.unitsTime}.
</pl-hint>
</pl-solution-panel>

A simple gas cycle compresses air from ${{params.Pressure1}}$ ${{params.unitsPressure}}$ to a pressure of ${{params.Pressure2}}$ ${{params.unitsPressure}}$ producing ${{params.OldQin}}$ ${{params.unitsMass}}$ of refrigeration.

The compressor and turbine efficiencies are ${{params.E1}}$% and ${{params.E2}}$%, and the maximum and minimum temperatures are ${{params.T3}} {{params.unitsTemperature}}$ and ${{params.T1}} {{params.unitsTemperature}}$.

Find the compressor's power and the cycle COP. (Assume k = 1.4)
solution.html:
The ideal compressor inlet temperature is $T_2^i$ = $T_3$*$\frac{P_2}{P_3}^\frac{k-1}{k}$ = {{params.T20}} {{params.unitsTemperatures}}. Since the compressor is {{params.E1}}% efficient, the actual inlet temperature $T_2$ is found as follows: $η_C$ = $\frac{c_p*(T_3 - T_2^i)} {c_p*(T_3 - T_2)}$ $\implies$ $T_2$ = $\frac{1}{η_C}$*($η_C$*$T_3$ - $T_3$ + $T_2^i$) = {{params.T2}}{{params.unitsTemperatures}}. The heat exhanger produces {{params.OldQin}} {{params.unitsMass}} of refrigeration which equals {{params.Qin}} {{params.unitsPowers}}.
  • We can now find $\dot{m}$ using the equation: $\dot{Q_i}$ = $\dot{m}$*$c_p$*($T_2$ - $T_1$). $\dot{m}$ = {{params.Mf}} {{params.unitsMassFlowRate}}.
  • The compressor power is then $\dot{W_c}$ = $\dot{m}$*$c_p$*($T_3$ - $T_2$) = {{correct_answers.Powerc}} {{params.unitsPower}}.
  • Ideal inlet temperature for the turbine: $T_4^i$ = $T_1$*$\frac{P_4}{P_1}^\frac{k-1}{k}$ = {{params.T40}} {{params.unitsTemperatures}}.
  • The actual inlet temperature for the turbine: $T_4$ = $η_T$*($T_4^i$ - $T_1$) + $T_1$ = {{params.T4}} {{params.unitsTemperatures}}.
  • The turbine power output is then $\dot{W_T}$ = $\dot{m}$*$c_p$*($T_4$ - $T_1$) = {{params.Powert}} {{params.unitsPower}}.
The cycle COP can now be calculated to be: COP = $\frac{\dot{Q_i}}{\dot{W}}$ = $\frac{\dot{Q_i}}{\dot{W_C} - \dot{W_T}}$ = {{correct_answers.COP}}.

  • $T_1$ = $T_4$*$(\frac{P_1}{P_4})^\frac{k-1}{k}$ = {{params.T4S}} * $(\frac{1}{ {{params.pr}} })^\frac{1.4-1}{1.4}$ = ... = {{correct_answers.T1}}${{params.unitsTemperature}}$
The COP can be calculated using the formula: COP = $\frac{ Q_{in} }{ W_{comp} - W_{turb} }$
  • $Q_{in}$ = $c_p$*($T_2$ - $T_1$) = {{params.cp}}*({{params.T2S}} - {{params.T1S}}) = {{params.Qin}} ${{params.unitsSpecificEnthalpy}}$

  • $W_{turb}$ = $c_p$*($T_4$ - $T_1$) = {{params.cp}}*({{params.T4S}} - {{params.T1S}}) = {{params.Wt}} ${{params.unitsSpecificEnthalpy}}$.
Finally, COP = {{correct_answers.COP}}

question.html:
A reversible power cycle receives {{params.Qh}} ${{params.unitsEnergy}}$ by heat transfer from a hot reservoir that's at {{params.T1}} ${{params.unitsTemperature}}$.

The power cycle rejects energy by heat transfer to a cold reservoir at temperature $T_c$, and has a thermal efficiency of {{params.Efficiency}} %.

Determine the energy rejected and $T_c$.
solution.html:
The thermal efficiency is given and can be expressed as: $η$ = $\frac{W}{Q_H}$ = $\frac{Q_H - Q_C}{Q_H}$ = 1 - $\frac{Q_C}{Q_H}$. Since the cycle is reversible, the thermal efficiency can aslo be expressed as: $η$ = 1 - $\frac{T_C}{T_H}$.
  • The energy rejected: $Q_C$ = (1 - $η$)*($Q_H$) = {{correct_answers.Qc}} ${{params.unitsEnergy}}$
  • Since cycle is reversible: $T_C$ = (1 - $η$)*($T_H$) = {{correct_answers.Tc}} ${{params.unitsTemperature}}$.

question.html:
Two reversible power cycles are in series aand each produce the same net work.

The first cycle accepts energy $Q_H$ from a hot reservoir that is at {{params.T1}} ${{params.unitsTemperature}}$ and reject energy Q to a reservoir at an intermediate temperature T by heat transfer.

The second cycle revceives energy Q from the reservior at T and rejects energy $Q_C$ to a reservoir at {{params.T2}} ${{params.unitsTemperature}}$ via heat transfer.

Determine the intermediate temperature and the thermal efficiencies.
solution.html:
Write the energy balance. Since $W_c$ is the net work developed by each cycle, $W_c$ = $Q_H$ - $Q$ = $Q$ - $Q_C$. Since the two cycles are reversible, $\frac{Q}{Q_H}$ = $\frac{T}{T_H}$ and $\frac{Q_C}{Q}$ = $\frac{T_C}{T}$.
  • Substituting in for $Q_H$ and $Q_C$: $Q$ = $\frac{\frac{T_H}{T}*Q + \frac{T_C}{T}*Q}{2}$.
  • Now we can solve for the intermediate temperature: T = $\frac{T_H + T_C}{2}$ = {{correct_answers.T}} ${{params.unitsTemperature}}$.
  • For a single reversible cycle operating between $T_H$ and $T_C$, the thermal efficiency is: $η$ = 1 - $\frac{T_C}{T_H}$.
  • For the first cycle, the intermediate temperature becomes the new cold temperature. So, the thermal efficiency for this cycle is: $η_1$ = 1 - $\frac{T}{T_H}$ = {{correct_answers.Efficiency1}}%
  • For the second cycle, the intermediate temperature becomes the new hot temperature. So, the thermal efficiency for this cycle is: $η_2$ = 1 - $\frac{T_C}{T}$ = {{correct_answers.Efficiency2}}%

To calculate the depreciation expense and the book value of the tape-drive system using the MACRS method, we first need to understand the depreciation rates associated with the property class. The MACRS depreciation method allows for accelerated depreciation, which means that more depreciation expense is recognized in the early years of the asset's life. The property class determines the applicable depreciation rates. For a {{params.propertyClass}}-year property, the MACRS rates can be found in the IRS guidelines. Typically, the rates for a 7-year property are approximately: 14.29%, 24.49%, 17.49%, 12.49%, 8.93%, 8.92%, 8.93%, and 4.46%. $\textbf{Depreciation Calculation and Book Values}$

The large tape-drive system for backing up computer servers is purchased for \( \text{Cost} = \text{{params.cost}} \). The MACRS depreciation percentages for a 7-year property are applied as follows:

\[ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Year} & \textbf{Depreciation Expense} & \textbf{Book Value at End of Year} \\ \hline \text{1} & {{params.dp1}} & {{correct_answers.bookValueEndYear1}} \\ \hline \text{2} & {{params.dp2}} & {{correct_answers.bookValueEndYear2}} \\ \hline \text{3} &{{params.dp3}} & {{correct_answers.bookValueEndYear3}} \\ \hline \text{4} & {{params.dp4}}& {{correct_answers.bookValueEndYear4}} \\ \hline \text{5} & {{params.dp5}} & {{correct_answers.bookValueEndYear5}} \\ \hline \text{6} & {{params.dp6}} & {{correct_answers.bookValueEndYear6}} \\ \hline \text{7} &{{params.dp7}} & {{correct_answers.bookValueEndYear7}} \\ \hline \text{8} & {{params.dp8}} & {{correct_answers.bookValueEndYear8}} \\ \hline \end{array} \] The tax payed for selling the autoclave for a salvage value of {{params.salvage}} at EOY 10 can be found as:

Tax Payed = ({{params.salavge}} - Book Value at EOY 10) $\times$ {{params.tax}}%

In our case, selling the autoclave at EOY 10 will provide a book value of zero.

Tax Payed = ({{params.salvage}} - 0) $\times$ {{params.tax}}% = {{correct_answers.taxLiability}}

 The tax payed for selling the autoclave for a salvage value of {{params.salvage}} at EOY {{params.year}} can be found as:

Tax Payed = ({{params.salvage}} - Book Value at EOY {{params.year}}) $\times$ {{params.tax}}%

In our case, selling the autoclave at EOY {{params.year}} will provide a book value of {{params.bvyear}}.

Tax Payed = ({{params.salvage}} - {{params.bvyear}}) $\times$ {{params.tax}}% = {{correct_answers.taxpayed}}

 The tax payed for selling the autoclave for a salvage value of {{params.salvage}} at EOY {{params.year}} can be found as:

Tax Payed = ({{params.salvageLow}} - Book Value at EOY {{params.year}}) $\times$ {{params.tax}}%

In our case, selling the autoclave at EOY {{params.year}} will provide a book value of {{params.bvyear}}.

Tax Payed = ({{params.salvageLow}} - {{params.bvyear}}) $\times$ {{params.tax}}% = {{correct_answers.taxpayedLow}}

Create a table showing the depreciation and book value for each year (i.e., from EOY 0 through EOY {{params.life_span}}) using straight-line depreciation. What is the book value at EOY {{params.mid}} and EOY {{params.eoy}}?
solution.html:
To calculate the depreciation and book value of the milling machine, we will use the straight-line depreciation method. The annual depreciation expense can be calculated using the formula: \[ \text{Depreciation Expense} = \frac{\text{Initial Cost} - \text{Salvage Value} }{\text{Life Span} } \] where the Initial Cost is {{params.initial_cost}} USD, the Salvage Value is {{params.salvage_value}} USD, and the Life Span is {{params.life_span}} years. After calculating the depreciation expense, we can determine the book value at the end of each year using the formula: \[ \text{Book Value at EOY} = \text{Initial Cost} - (\text{Depreciation Expense} \times \text{Number of Years}) \] We will create a table to show the depreciation and book value from EOY 0 through EOY {{params.life_span}}:

question.html:
Given the following cash flow details for the year 2018:

  • Before-Tax-and-Loan-Cash-Flow = {{params.before_tax_and_loan_cash_flow}}
  • Payment on loan principal = {{params.loan_principal_payment}}
  • Payment on loan interest = {{params.loan_interest_payment}}
  • MACRS Depreciation Deduction = {{params.macrs_depreciation_deduction}}
  • Taxrate = {{params.tax}}%

    • What is the taxable income for ACME Inc?

    What is the Tax Payed?

    What is the after tax cash flow, (ATCF)?
solution.html:
To calculate the taxable income for ACME Inc., we start with the Before-Tax-and-Loan Cash Flow and deduct the payments made on loan principal, loan interest, and the MACRS depreciation deduction. The formula for taxable income can be expressed as: \[ \text{Taxable Income} = \text{Before-Tax-and-Loan Cash Flow} - \text{Loan Interest Payment} - \text{MACRS Depreciation Deduction} \] Substituting the known values: \[ \text{Taxable Income} = {{params.before_tax_and_loan_cash_flow}} - {{params.loan_interest_payment}} - {{params.macrs_depreciation_deduction}} \] The final taxable income for ACME Inc. is thus calculated as follows: \[ \text{Taxable Income} = {{params.before_tax_and_loan_cash_flow}} - {{params.loan_interest_payment}} - {{params.macrs_depreciation_deduction}} = {{correct_answers.taxable}} \]

The tax payed is the taxable income multiplied by the tax rate.

Tax Payed = {{correct_answers.taxable}} $\times$ {{params.tax}}%= {{correct_answers.taxPayed}}

 The after tax cash flow (ATCF) can be found as: ATCF = BTLCF - Tax Payed - Expenses

In our case the expenses is just the principle payed.

AFTC = {{params.before_tax_and_loan_cash_flow}} - {{correct_answers.taxPayed}} - {{params.loan_principal_payment}} = {{correct_answers.ATCF}}

question.html:
Through a turbine, air expands from a pressure of {{params.Pressure1}} ${{params.unitsPressure}}$ and a temperature of {{params.T1}} ${{params.unitsTemperature}}$ to {{params.Pressure2}} ${{params.unitsPressure}}$ and {{params.T2}} ${{params.unitsTemperature}}$. The exit

velocity, which is {{params.Vel2}} ${{params.unitsSpeed}}$, is much faster than the entrance velocity. The turbine generates {{params.Power}} ${{params.unitsPower}}$ while it is operating

in steady state. Heat transfer between the turbine and its surroundings and any potential energy effects are negligible.

Calculate the air's mass flow rate and exit area using an ideal gas model of air.
solution.html:
Write the energy rate balance for this problem. At steady state, the energy rate balance can be written as: 0 = $\dot{Q}$ - $\dot{W}$ + $\dot{m}$*($h_1$ - $h_2$ + $\frac{V_1^2 - V_2^2}{2}$ + g*($z_1$ - $z_2$)).
  • Neglecting heat transfer and potential energy effects, and setting $V_1$ = 0, the energy rate balance can be reduced to: 0 = - $\dot{W}$ + $\dot{m}$*($h_1$ - $h_2$ + $\frac{- V_2^2}{2}$).
  • To find the mass flow rate ($\dot{m}$), the energy rate balance can be rearranged: $\dot{m}$ = $\frac{\dot{W}}{h_1 - h_2 + \frac{- V_2^2}{2}}$ = $\frac{\dot{W}}{c_p*(T_1 - T_2) + \frac{- V_2^2}{2}}$
  • The mass flow rate can be expressed as: $\dot{m}$ = $\frac{A_2*V_2}{v_2}$ (where $v_2$ is the specific volume).
  • For the ideal gas equation, P*$v$ = R*T, the specific volume can be expressed as $v$ = $\frac{R*T}{P}$ (where R is the gas constant).
  • The mass flow rate can now be written as: $\dot{m}$ = $\frac{A_2*V_2*P_2}{R*T_2}$.
  • Solving for the mass flow rate should give: $\dot{m}$ = {{correct_answers.Mf}} ${{params.unitsMassFlowRate}}$.
  • Solving for exit area, $A_2$ = $\frac{\dot{m}*R*T_2}{V_2*P_2}$ = {{correct_answers.A2}} ${{params.unitsArea}}$.

question.html:
Air at ${{params.Pressure1}}$ ${{params.unitsPressure}}$ and ${{params.T1}}$${{params.unitsTemperature}}$ enters a turbojet engine with an inlet velocity of {{params.Vel1}} {{params.unitsSpeed}}.

The compressor discharge pressure is ${{params.Pressure2}}$ ${{params.unitsPressure}}$ and the turbine inlet temperature is ${{params.T3}} {{params.unitsTemperature}}$.

The air mass flow rate is {{params.MF}} {{params.unitsMassFlowRate}} and kinetic energy is negligible except at the inlet and exit of the engine.

Determine the exit velocity and the thrust developed by the engine.
solution.html:
• The energy equation can be applied across the nozzle as: $(\frac{V_4}{2})^2$ + $h_4$ = $(\frac{V_5}{2})^2$ + $h_5$.
  • This equation can then be reduced to find the exit velocity: $V_5$ = $[2*c_p*(T_4 - T_5)]^{1/2}$
  • To solve the energy equation, we must find $T_4$ and $T_5$. Lets start with $T_4$.
  • Since the work from the turbine is the same as the work required by the compressor: $h_2$ - $h_1$ = $h_3$ - $h_4$ $\implies$ $T_2$ - $T_1$ = $T_3$ - $T_4$.
  • Assuming isentropic compression and expansion: $T_2$ = $T_1$*$(\frac{P_2}{P_1})^\frac{k-1}{k}$ = {{params.T2}}{{params.unitsTemperatures}}.
  • $T_4$ = $T_3$ - ($T_2$ - $T_1$) = {{params.T4}}{{params.unitsTemperatures}}.
  • Assuming an isentropic process, $T_5$ at the nozzle exit (where $P_5$ = {{params.Pressure1}} {{params.unitsPressure}}) is: $T_5$ = $T_4$*$(\frac{P_5}{P_4})^\frac{k-1}{k}$
  • The isentropic expansion through the turbine shows: $P_4$ = $P_3$*$(\frac{T_4}{T_3})^\frac{k}{k-1}$ = {{params.Pressure4}} {{params.unitsPressure}}
  • Now, $T_5$ = {{params.T5}}{{params.unitsTemperatures}}.
 After doing necessary conversions, the exit velocity is: $V_5$ = $[2*c_p*(T_4 - T_5)]^{1/2}$ = {{correct_answers.Vel5}} {{params.unitsSpeed}}. After doing necessary conversions, the thrust is: thrust = $\dot{m}$*($V_5$ - $V_1$) = {{correct_answers.Thrust}}{{params.unitsForce}}.
